kangaroo-at-2010-junior-02.title: Percent difference
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-02.body:
The difference between Tibor and Ivan is $90\% - 85\% = 5\%$ of the maximum, and this is 1 point. So the maximum is $1 \div 0.05 = 20$ points.

**Answer: (D) 20**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-02.title: Check the choices
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-02.body:
With 20 points: Ivan has $17$, Tibor $18$ — exactly one more. ✓

**Answer: (D) 20**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-03.title: Compare column by column
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-03.body:
Each of the first ten numbers in the bottom row is 10 more than the one above it, so the bottom row is ahead by $10\cdot 10 = 100$ in these columns. To make the sums equal, the question mark must be $100$ less than 2010: $1910$.

**Answer: (C) 1910**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-04.title: Count the visible faces
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-04.body:
Each cube face has area $24 \div 6 = 4\text{ cm}^2$. The object is a $2\times2\times1$ block: front and back $4 + 4$ faces, and around the edge $2$ faces on each of the 4 sides, so $16$ faces in total: $16\cdot 4 = 64\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: (B) $64\text{ cm}^2$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-04.title: Subtract hidden faces
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-04.body:
Four cubes have $4\cdot 24 = 96\text{ cm}^2$. There are 4 places where two cubes touch, each hiding 2 faces: $96 - 8\cdot 4 = 64\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: (B) $64\text{ cm}^2$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-05.title: Triangular numbers
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-05.body:
She has $1 + 2 + \dots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = 120$ roses, so $n(n+1) = 240 = 15\cdot 16$: she is 15.

**Answer: (D) 15**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-06.title: Find each figure
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-06.body:
Use grid coordinates (left to right $x$, bottom to top $y$). The points are $P(5,5)$, $Q(2,4)$, $R(6,4)$, $S(0,2)$, $T(4,2)$, $U(2,0)$.

- **Square:** $Q, T, U, S$ — each side goes 2 across and 2 up/down, and the sides are perpendicular.
- **Parallelogram with unequal sides:** $S, T, R, Q$ — $ST$ and $QR$ are horizontal of length 4, $SQ$ and $TR$ are both "2 right, 2 up" (length $2\sqrt2$).
- **Acute triangle:** $P, S, U$ — $PS^2 = 25 + 9 = 34$, $PU^2 = 9 + 25 = 34$, $SU^2 = 8$; isosceles with a short base, so all angles are acute.
- **Obtuse triangle:** $S, T, R$ — at $T$ the directions to $S$ (left) and to $R$ (right and up) make an angle of $135^\circ$.

All figures are possible.

**Answer: (E) all figures are possible**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-07.title: Count the odd numbers
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-07.body:
The picture shows that the first $n$ odd numbers add up to $n\times n$ (each odd number adds an L-shaped layer to the square). From 1 to 19 there are 10 odd numbers, so the sum is $10\times 10$.

**Answer: (A) $10\times 10$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-08.title: Even and at least 5
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-08.body:
She ends on the same side of the river where she started, so she crosses the river an even number of times. She crosses each of the five bridges at least once, so $n \ge 5$. Among the choices only $6$ is even and at least 5 (e.g. cross bridges 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and then bridge 1 again).

**Answer: (D) 6**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-11.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-11.body:
Put $A = (0,0)$, $B = (1,0)$, $C = (1,1)$, $E = (0,1)$. The apex $D$ of the equilateral triangle on $EC$ (outside the square) is $\left(\frac12, 1 + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$, and $F$ (on $BC$, inside the square) is $\left(1 - \frac{\sqrt3}2, \frac12\right)$.
$$FD^2 = \left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} - \tfrac12\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + \tfrac12\right)^2 = 2\left(\tfrac34 + \tfrac14\right) = 2,$$
so $FD = \sqrt2$.

**Answer: (A) $\sqrt2$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-11.title: Angles at C
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-11.body:
$CF = CB = 1$ and $CD = CE = 1$. The angle $FCD$ equals $\angle FCE + \angle ECD = (90^\circ - 60^\circ) + 60^\circ = 90^\circ$. So $FCD$ is a right isosceles triangle with legs 1 and $FD = \sqrt2$.

**Answer: (A) $\sqrt2$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-13.title: Factor 2010
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-13.body:
$2010 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 67$. The ages must be realistic factor pairs: $1\cdot2010$, $2\cdot1005$, $3\cdot670$, $5\cdot402$, $6\cdot335$, $10\cdot201$, $15\cdot134$, $30\cdot67$, … Only $30$ (teacher) and $67$ (father) are plausible. In 2010 the teacher is 30, so he was born in 1980.

**Answer: (C) 1980**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-14.title: Angle sums in two triangles
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-14.body:
The reflex angle of $330^\circ$ at the top means the angle at the top vertex $T$ is $360^\circ - 330^\circ = 30^\circ$. Let $L$ be the bottom-left vertex (with the $20^\circ$), $R$ the bottom-right vertex (with the ?), and $X$ the crossing point of the two inner lines, where the angle is $90^\circ$. The line from $R$ meets the left side at $Q$.

In triangle $LXQ$: $\angle QLX = 20^\circ$ and $\angle LXQ = 90^\circ$, so $\angle LQX = 70^\circ$. Hence $\angle TQR = 180^\circ - 70^\circ = 110^\circ$.

In triangle $TQR$: $? = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 110^\circ = 40^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) $40^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-14.title: Quadrilateral around the crossing
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-14.body:
The line from $L$ meets the right side at $P$. In triangle $TLP$: $\angle TPL = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 20^\circ = 130^\circ$. In triangle $RXP$, the angle at $X$ is $90^\circ$ and the angle at $P$ is $180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ$, so the angle at $R$ is $180^\circ - 90^\circ - 50^\circ = 40^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) $40^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-15.title: Digits are 1s and one 2
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-15.body:
A digit product of 2 means one digit is 2 and all others are 1 (no 0s). The digit sum is then $2 + (\text{number of 1s}) = 2010$, so there are 2008 ones and 2009 digits in all. The 2 can be in any of the 2009 positions: $2009$ numbers.

**Answer: (B) 2009**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-16.title: Through the 3 or not
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-16.body:
The numbers form a $3\times3$ block
$$\begin{array}{ccc}1&2&1\\2&3&2\\1&2&1\end{array}$$
and every path from A to B goes from the bottom-left 1 to the top-right 1, moving right or up, stepping on 5 numbers.

- If the path uses the centre 3, it steps on a corner 1, an edge 2, the 3, an edge 2, a corner 1: sum $9$.
- Otherwise it runs along the edges: $1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7$.

So only 2 different results: 7 and 9.

**Answer: (B) 2**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-17.title: Find the Tuesdays
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-17.body:
Consecutive Tuesdays alternate between odd and even dates (7 is odd). Three even Tuesdays need five Tuesdays in the month, with the 1st, 3rd and 5th even: dates $d, d+14, d+28$ with $d$ even and $d + 28 \le 31$, so $d = 2$.

The Tuesdays are the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th. The 21st is two days before Tuesday the 23rd: **Sunday**.

**Answer: (E) Sunday**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-18.title: Add up the arcs
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-18.body:
Each part is bounded by a quarter of the big circle, $\frac14\cdot 2\pi\cdot 4 = 2\pi$, and by two of the semicircles, each $\pi\cdot 2 = 2\pi$. Perimeter $= 2\pi + 2\pi + 2\pi = 6\pi$ cm.

**Answer: (C) $6\pi$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-18.title: Total length
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-18.body:
All the lines together: big circle $8\pi$ plus four semicircles $4\cdot 2\pi = 8\pi$. Every semicircle borders two parts, the big circle borders each part once, so the four perimeters add up to $8\pi + 2\cdot 8\pi = 24\pi$, i.e. $6\pi$ each.

**Answer: (C) $6\pi$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-19.title: Steepest line from the origin
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-19.body:
Average speed is distance ÷ time, which is the slope of the line from the origin $0$ to the student's point. The steepest such line goes to Doris: she covered almost as much distance as Chris in much less time, and more than Bernd in about the same time. So Doris was fastest.

**Answer: (D) Doris**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-20.title: Single and double layers
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-20.body:
Let the triangle have area $T$. The folded figure has area $\frac{T}{1.5} = \frac{2T}{3}$. Folding makes a doubled region (where the flap lies on the rest) and the area lost is exactly the area of this overlap: overlap $= T - \frac{2T}{3} = \frac T3$.

The folded figure = overlap + single-layer (grey) parts, so the grey parts have area $\frac{2T}{3} - \frac{T}{3} = \frac T3 = 1$, giving $T = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-21.title: What one extra trolley adds
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-21.body:
Ten more trolleys add $4.9 - 2.9 = 2$ m, so each extra trolley pushed in adds $0.2$ m. A row of 10 is one full trolley plus 9 additions: $L + 9\cdot 0.2 = 2.9$, so $L = 1.1$ m.

**Answer: (C) 1.1 m**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-21.title: Equations
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-21.body:
If one trolley is $L$ long and each additional trolley adds $x$: $L + 9x = 2.9$ and $L + 19x = 4.9$. Subtracting: $10x = 2$, $x = 0.2$, $L = 1.1$ m.

**Answer: (C) 1.1 m**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-22.title: Subtract the corner triangles
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-22.body:
The big triangle has side 6. Reading the picture: $A$ is on the left side 1 unit above the bottom-left corner, $B$ is on the bottom side 4 units from the bottom-left corner, and $C$ is on the right side 3 units above the bottom-right corner (i.e. 3 units from the top).

Cut off the three pieces of the big triangle outside $ABC$. A triangle with two sides $a$, $b$ along the sides of the big triangle at a $60^\circ$ corner has area $ab$ small triangles (since a $1\times1$ such triangle is one small triangle and area scales with $ab$).
- Bottom-left corner: sides $1$ and $4$ → $4$.
- Bottom-right corner: sides $2$ and $3$ → $6$.
- Top corner: sides $5$ (down the left side to $A$) and $3$ (down the right side to $C$) → $15$.

Area $ABC = 36 - 4 - 6 - 15 = 11\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: (A) $11\text{ cm}^2$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-22.title: Lattice coordinates
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-22.body:
Use oblique coordinates with unit vectors along the bottom side and the left side; one unit "parallelogram" equals 2 small triangles. Then $A = (0,1)$, $B = (4,0)$, $C = (3,3)$ and
$$\text{area} = \tfrac12\left|\det\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\right| = \tfrac{11}{2}\text{ parallelograms} = 11 \text{ small triangles}.$$

**Answer: (A) $11\text{ cm}^2$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-23.title: Strip areas are odd numbers
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-23.body:
Measure areas in units of the small top triangle. The triangle formed by the top $k$ strips is similar with ratio $k$, so its area is $k^2$. The $k$-th strip therefore has area $k^2 - (k-1)^2 = 2k - 1$: $1, 3, 5, \dots, 19$, total $100$.

In the picture the grey strips are the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th from the top: $1 + 5 + 9 + 13 + 17 = 45$, i.e. $45\%$.

**Answer: (C) 45 %**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-24.title: Even and odd n
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-24.body:
- If $n$ is even, $n^n = \left(n^{n/2}\right)^2$ is a square: 50 numbers.
- If $n$ is odd, $n^n$ is a square exactly when $n$ itself is a square (each prime exponent of $n$ is multiplied by the odd number $n$, so it stays odd if it was odd): $1, 9, 25, 49, 81$ — 5 numbers.

Total $55$.

**Answer: (C) 55**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-25.title: At most one tells the truth
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-25.body:
The four statements contradict each other, so at most one octopus tells the truth.

If all four lied, all would have 7 legs, 28 in total — and then blue's statement would be true. Contradiction.

So exactly one tells the truth and the other three have 7 legs each: the total is $21 + 6 = 27$ or $21 + 8 = 29$. Only 27 is claimed, so the green one is the truthful (six-legged) octopus, and the red one is a liar with **7** legs.

**Answer: (B) 7**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-27.title: Find the pattern
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-27.body:
Continue: $a_8 = 5 + (-2) - 7 = -4$, $a_9 = -2 + 7 - (-4) = 9$, $a_{10} = 7 - 4 - 9 = -6$, …

Odd terms: $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, \dots$ so $a_n = n$. Even terms: $2, 0, -2, -4, -6, \dots$ so $a_n = 4 - n$.

(Check: these formulas satisfy $a_n = a_{n-3} + a_{n-2} - a_{n-1}$ for both parities.) Hence $a_{2010} = 4 - 2010 = -2006$.

**Answer: (A) $-2006$**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-28.title: Each number needs two primes
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-28.body:
Take any side $s$. The two sides not adjacent to $s$ are adjacent to each other, so they are coprime. $s$ shares a factor with each of them — these must be two **different** primes $p \ne q$ (a common prime would divide both of them). So every number on the pentagon has at least two different prime factors.

$19$ is prime, so it can never appear. (15, 18, 21, 22 each have two prime factors and do fit into suitable examples.)

**Answer: (C) 19**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-29.title: First and last digits of equal parity
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-29.body:
For $\overline{abc}$ we need $2b = a + c$; this works exactly when $a$ and $c$ have the same parity (then $b = \frac{a+c}{2}$ is a digit automatically).
- $a$ odd (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and $c$ odd: $5\cdot 5 = 25$
- $a$ even (2, 4, 6, 8) and $c$ even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8): $4\cdot 5 = 20$

Total $45$.

**Answer: (E) 45**

kangaroo-at-2010-junior-30.title: Count by number of stripes
kangaroo-at-2010-junior-30.body:
The colours are fixed by the number of stripes, which must be odd (black at both ends). With $m$ stripes, of which $j$ have width 2: $m + j = 12$, $j \le m$.
- $m = 7$, $j = 5$: $\binom75 = 21$
- $m = 9$, $j = 3$: $\binom93 = 84$
- $m = 11$, $j = 1$: $\binom{11}{1} = 11$

Total $21 + 84 + 11 = 116$.

**Answer: (E) 116**
